Coping with 54C heat: Delhi slum diaries detail living in extreme temperatures


With heatwaves now recognised as disasters, personal testimonies are key to a new project that looks to protect those living in the most cramped districts of India’s capital




Every summer evening, Gulshan follows the same routine. She washes the floor of her one-room home several times so it cools a little for her four children to sleep on. Last summer, the family saved enough to buy a desert cooler, which uses evaporation as a cheaper alternative to air conditioning.
The family uses the appliance cautiously to save on energy costs. But even when it is on, Gulshan, who does not use a surname, has to dampeneveryone’s clothes before sleeping. The 39-year-old and her children now have rashes and one has a skin infection from the wet cloth against their skin.



View image in fullscreen
Gulshan writes in her heat diary. Photograph: Suchitra
This summer, Gulshan started jotting down these coping strategies in a garmi khata, or heat registry. “I feel relieved that at least somebody might read my family’s experiences,” she says.
They are one of 40 households in Sunder Nagri, a slum in north-east Delhi, documenting their experiences of surviving the city’s increasingly longer and more frequent heatwaves.
Over the last few years, cities across India have begun drawing up heat action plans – agreements formulated by a municipality or district administration on how to prepare for and respond to extreme heat.
While some incorporate data such as satellite-derived land surface temperatures to identify heat hotspots, there are still significant gaps in information on people, making it difficult to understand how heat is experienced differently across communities.
Aravind Unni, an urban planner and researcher in Delhi, says: “Experiences of heat are vastly different depending on geography, income, occupation, gender, caste, class.
“While we have some meteorological data on heat, what’s absolutely missing is people, community – what they feel, what they experience.”

A thermal image of Sunder Nagri’s main market area, showing a ground temperature of 54.1C (129.4F). Photograph: Sabique Ahmed/Greenpeace
Most data collated in heat planning is usually just meteorological, such as air temperatures and heatwave thresholds.. The idea for the heat diaries was to “move beyond just the numbers”, says Nibedita Saha, a Greenpeace India researcher who worked on the project.

articles.title: Rain on way for UK with temperatures to drop to overnight lows of 3C in some places
articles.raw_rss: After and exceptional summer of heatwaves and drought, the weather will turn wetter and cooler this week, as Simon King explains
articles.raw_meta: After and exceptional summer of heatwaves and drought, the weather will turn wetter and cooler this week, as Simon King explains
articles.jina_text:
Wisley in Surrey has notched up 60 days with no recorded rainfall. Significant rain has been lacking elsewhere with most areas of England and Wales in drought.
There is some welcome rain forecast this week, though it's not likely to be significant or bring any change to the dry conditions.
It will also turn noticeably cooler in the coming days with temperatures falling below average across the UK.





Image caption, 

Rainfall accumulation over the next five days shows a chance of some rainfall for most of the UK, though no significant amount in southern England




High pressure has been dominant this summer leading to hot and dry weather, particularly across England and Wales.
There's been no significant rain in southern England for around two months which has led water levels in our rivers and reservoirs to drop significantly. All of Wales and most of England are in drought.
However, through this week high pressure will be replaced by the influence of low pressure and more unsettled conditions.
Some light rain is likely on Monday, mostly across northern areas of the UK.
Into Tuesday and Wednesday this will turn heavier and start to move into southern England.
While rain is therefore finally going to fall across the south, it may become more showery. This means the exact location and distribution of rainfall is still uncertain.
And while of course any rain will be welcome, it won't bring much improvement to conditions.
It will take weeks of above average rainfall into the autumn to make any significant changes to the drought.
However, it is likely to make a big difference to the emergency services who have been battling against the extreme weather and wildfires over the last few weeks.
The fire severity index - how severe a fire could be, should one start - will come down to low or moderate, according to forecasts from Natural England and the Met Office.






How much rain will end the drought?





6 August


Fires prompt national alert as 19 homes destroyed





2 days ago





Image caption, 

Temperatures will fall below average - indicated by the blue hue on map above - through this week



Turning much cooler




On Saturday the temperature peaked at 30.6C in southern England, making it the 40th day somewhere in the UK over 30C this year.
It's looking unlikely temperatures will peak this high again for the rest of the summer, which meteorologically ends on 31 August.
Temperatures on Monday and Tuesday will still be above average across England and Wales with highs of 20 to 26C.
But they will drop during the rest of the week as a mostly northerly airflow starts to have more influence.
By the end of the week, temperatures across the UK will be around 2 to 4C below average. Something we haven't seen much - if really at all - this summer.
Across Scotland and Northern Ireland temperatures will be around 14-17C and for England and Wales, 17-21C.
Nights will become much cooler, and in some part, even colder, too.

articles.raw_meta: Loggerhead turtles abound this season but rollback of Endangered Species Act protections could threaten future
articles.jina_text:
Wildlife groups in Florida are celebrating record numbers of sea turtle nests this season, but experts warn Donald Trump’s recent gutting of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) could reverse decades of their recovery from the edge of extinction.
With more than two months of the summer nesting season still to run, loggerhead turtles have already made 13,770 nests, hundreds more than recorded in any previous year, along an 8.5-mile stretch of shoreline monitored by the Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach, on Florida’s Atlantic coast.

The same record has fallen on Sanibel island, on the Gulf coast, where loggerheads have laid 922 nests so far this year, surpassing the 2023 total of 878, according to the Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation.
The numbers reflect the ongoing revival of sea turtles since the 1970s, when overhunting, poaching and habitat loss pushed several species to the brink, including the loss of about 95% of the Caribbean’s population of green turtles.


View image in fullscreen
A sea turtle is prepared for a CT scan at the Loggerhead Marinelife Center. Photograph: Loggerhead Marinelife Center
The ESA, passed in 1973, enshrined protections that are paying dividends now because sea turtle hatchlings take years to decades to reach reproductive age. The loss of those safeguards, from Trump’s “death sentence” repeal last month of sections of the law to favor oil drilling, mining, logging and development interests, has some experts fearful that the recovery might have reached the high-water mark.


An alliance of environmental and wildlife groups is suing the Trump administration in part over a rule giving outsized deference to “economic considerations” when determining protections for endangered species and critical habitat.
“What we’re seeing is the result of several decades of sustained protection of these species under the ESA and various other measures to protect their habitat in different ways,” said David Godfrey, executive director of the Sea Turtle Conservancy, an advocacy group that is not a plaintiff in the lawsuit, but is supportive of it.
“It takes just about any species of sea turtle 20, 30 years to reach maturity, to come back and nest, to return to beaches where they were first protected as eggs or as hatchlings and afforded the opportunity to live without ending up in a fisherman’s net and on a table in a nice restaurant.
“So the recovery’s going on largely due to the ESA, which is one of the reasons why we’re all very concerned about the setbacks to the legislation.”
The ESA is credited with safeguarding more than 1,700 species and their habitats, preventing 99% of those listed from going extinct.
Godfrey said: “The detractors of the ESA sometimes say, ‘Oh, this thing is a failure. Look at all these animals that are still on the list. We haven’t removed a lot from the list.’ And I come right back and say, yeah, but look at all these animals that are on the list that we haven’t lost.

articles.jina_text:
Nurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plans





I don’t think I have ever written before about a British strike directly related to the climate emergency. But that’s exactly what began late last week in north London, with a zeitgeisty connection to Andy Burnham’s fixation on buses: picket lines outside depots and massed walkouts, while the temperatures in the relevant parts of the capital and its suburbs hovered at about 34C (93F).
Last Friday, more than 1,500 drivers employed by the transport giant Arriva began a planned run of 26 stoppages through to October, affecting bus routes spread between London and Essex. Everything is being led by the union Unite, whose recent grievances include alleged company union-busting and assaults by the public on staff. But the fundamental basis of the dispute is at the heart of the national condition: the near-impossibility for millions of people of working through another insanely hot summer.



Most of Arriva North London’s buses, says Unite, have old-fashioned air cooling systems rather than air conditioning, which means that onboard temperatures have come down by only two or three degrees during this year’s five heatwaves. On other such vehicles, it insists, the air-con is broken. The cabs where drivers sit are essentially compact greenhouses, and can easily reach 40C or higher. And there is another grim twist: union members complain of a shortage of toilets on too many routes, meaning they refrain from drinking water. Unite has been warning about all this since the phases of intense heat that began back in May; its members, the union says, have experienced “heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration”.
Arriva’s last financial figures showed a pre-tax profit of £133m. The company insists that it has “introduced short-term measures to protect drivers”, and is now also spending money on “longer-term fixes, including cab air-conditioning upgrades and our ongoing investment in new fleet”. But the root of its current problems seem clear. There is a longstanding failure, which runs across the UK’s public and private sectors – and also transcends national boundaries – to understand the mounting everyday effects of global heating, and to engage in what so many 21st-century companies and institutions remain so bad at: protective investment, with both eyes fixed not just on the searing inevitabilities of the future, but realities that are already here.


Arriva places tight restrictions on its drivers talking to the media, so Unite pointed me instead to Mo, who has worked for another London bus operator for over 15 years, and had come to a picket line to show the strikers his support. “When it’s very hot, it’s very difficult to concentrate,” he told me. “Imagine the heat you feel when you put your hand near an oven. articles.title: ‘It is not only a future certainty – the disaster is already here’: why we need climate fiction
articles.raw_rss: As wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisisEarlier this summer, I travelled through Europe on a book tour. As wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisis




Earlier this summer, I travelled through Europe on a book tour. Everywhere I went, the heat broke records. In Italy, Germany and Spain, I sought refuge from the afternoon sun in air-conditioned hotels. In normally temperate Zurich, it averaged 37 degrees. I jumped into the Limmat for relief. On my final day in Warsaw, Poland had never been hotter – one of 14 countries to hit a historic high. In June, when I left to return to the US, Europe was scorching. At the end of July, as I write this, it is burning.
Since the heatwaves began, there have been more than 10,000 excess deaths. Yet for many, myself included, the high temperatures brought nothing more than inconvenience – uncomfortable commutes, heat rash, less time outdoors. This seems to be a defining feature of today’s climate crisis; deadly for some, banal for others. Even when the world is on fire, it somehow doesn’t feel like an emergency for everyone.

This disparity cast my mind back to Hurricane Sandy in 2012. I was living in New York, one of millions ordered to shelter in place. (I was lucky – hundreds of thousands were ordered to evacuate their homes.) I followed instructions. I stayed in my warm, dry apartment on the Upper West Side, watching trees swaying violently against the dark sky. The next morning, the rain had stopped; the sun was out, the air was still again and the power was still on. When I went outside to survey the damage, there was little to see except a few broken branches. The mood in my neighbourhood was jovial. The subways were closed, schools were shut, work was called off. Brunch was on.
In other parts of the city, it was a different story. Whole fleets of taxi cabs submerged in water, their canary yellow roofs peeking out; a huge midtown crane snapped cleanly in half; the collapsed wall of an apartment building. I watched and rewatched a video of a power plant exploding. Half a million people, including most of the residents of lower Manhattan, were now without electricity. The American news outlets focused almost exclusively on New York. The international news sites told a more complete story: Sandy killed 233 people in eight countries and caused $70bn in damage.
Several days after the storm, I volunteered in Chinatown, distributing basic goods – batteries, canned food and bottled water – to elderly people who lived on the highest floors of public housing buildings and hadn’t yet ventured outside since the storm. (the lifts weren’t working and they weren’t able to take the stairs). The apartments smelled of rotting food and unflushed toilets. Two decades ago, economist Sir Nicholas Stern was asked by then chancellor Gordon Brown to carry out a review on the economics of climate change. The 700-page document that he produced would become a landmark shift in how climate change is framed: that it is an economic issue, and not just an environmental issue; that the cost of inaction is far greater than the cost of action; and that climate change is "the greatest market failure the world has seen". 
The Stern Review would go on to shape UK and EU climate policy for decades, helping to mainstream key decarbonisation tools such as carbon pricing and green investment. The years since have seen the price of green technologies plummet and major achievements like the 2015 Paris Agreement, which has given the world a framework for decarbonisation. But there has also been another, less positive story: of emissions continuing to rise year-on-year, and of extreme weather resulting from the climate crisis shifting from a future problem to a present emergency.
Given this contradictory context, how does Lord Stern view his own assessment, two decades on?
“Well, at the time we were accused of being alarmist, but in fact we understated the risks,” he tells The Independent, speaking over Zoom this week. “Every time a major new scientific report has come out, the climate crisis looks worse… 20 years ago we thought the British local surface temperature relative to the second half 19th century might go up by 0.2C per decade, but had that been true, we would be at about 1.2C now, while instead we are at 1.4C or 1.5C.” 




At the same time, low-carbon technologies have delivered far greater opportunities than were originally anticipated, only strengthening the Stern Review’s central argument, suggests Stern. 

“We did not anticipate 20 years ago that round-the-clock renewables would become cheaper than dirty energy, and we did not anticipate that the rise of electric vehicles would mean we are approaching the end of the era of the internal combustion engine,” he says. Other, harder to decarbonise sectors - including heavy industry and aviation - can follow a similar price trajectory with the same formula of helpful state regulation and investment resulting in technological improvements, he says. 


One constant across the many decades of the climate movement has been a well-funded climate-sceptic lobby, determined to dismiss the logic of the green transition and undercut its arguments. That lobby's strength has, despite ever-more alarming extreme weather, only grown in recent years - with a climate sceptic president now in the White House, and figures from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to former Labour prime minister Tony Blair (whose government commissioned the Stern Review) souring on the UK's net z

Fire has always be part of life on the grasslands, but has grown worse due to rising temperatures and severe droughts. In response, people have turned to their nomadic heritage to help tackle the blazes



By Michael O Snyder




Sodnomjamts Damchaabadgar squats in a shallow, rocky depression, working quietly with his hands. Inches above the rim of the pit, the wind whips across the grasslands. But in the marginal shelter of the dig site the air remains calm – essential for delicate operations.
Damchaabadgar, a research fellow at the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, has erected a ger, a traditional nomad’s tent, nearby, which serves as his sleeping quarters and a field station.



View image in fullscreen

 
 
Two gers stand alone against the vast openness of the steppe in Eastern Mongolia. The ger – often called a yurt outside Mongolia – is a round dwelling designed to be assembled or disassembled in a matter of hours 


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Sodnomtsamts Damchaabadgar excavates a pair of skulls from a bronze age burial site in Aduun Chuluun, Töv province 
“When we examine these gravesites, we see evidence of horse domestication dating back to the middle bronze age,” he says. “We now think that the ancient peoples of Mongolia may have tamed horses far earlier than previously expected, perhaps as early as 2,000 BCE, which makes sense because horses were critical to survival on the grasslands. They gave an advantage in battle – that’s well known – but perhaps just as importantly, horses gave them the speed that they needed to escape from the grassland’s greatest natural threat: fire.”


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Fire rangers arrive on the scene of a blaze in Bayan-Ovoo, Khentii province

Left: the remnants of a burned ger in Dornod province. Right: a faint scar from a recent fire crosses a rural road 


While fire has long been endemic on the steppe, the hazard has been steadily growing in the 20th and 21st centuries. The human-driven climate crisis has led to the heating and drying of the Eurasian grasslands, with a 2C rise in temperatures recorded over the last 80 years.

articles.jina_text:
Viewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaign conclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this week flatly rejected his latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’s attacks on Nato allies grow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more.
Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His boss mocked him as “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner.



Or maybe not.
Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice: become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps.
Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. He lamented the decline of “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump has attacked eight countries in the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession, could be next.

Alarmed by the alarm: people react to ‘severe alert’ on phones over UK wildfires


Many complained online that piercingly loud tone was ‘overreach’ while others lamented lack of action on decarbonisation




On Friday at 7pm, Thérèse Coffey was nine miles away from a nuclear power station when her phone made a loud, piercing and very worrying sound: it was a “severe” emergency alert. “Was expecting [a] much more specific alert, not a generic message on wildfires,” the former Conservative cabinet minister said on X.
She wasn’t alone in being alarmed by the alarm sent to phones in England and Wales. In the aftermath, thousands of social media users expressed their shock at alert. Some shared funny memes and others lamented what they viewed as lack of government action on decarbonisation. Academic John Ritzema called it a “massive overreach” and said the alert system should be “be for ‘drop everything and prepare for something terrible’ situations”, something Coffey echoed, saying alerts should not become commonplace to avoid “Peter cries wolf situations”.



Even broadcasters were taken by surprise. The alert sounded live on the BBC’s The One Show, with host Ronan Kemp saying: “We’ve got some form of fire alarm going on.”
Chris Packham used the alert to plug a parliamentary petition calling for a UK-wide briefing on climate and nature risks.
The alert on Friday night came as Andy Burnham spent time in Stourbridge in the West Midlands earlier that day after homes were destroyed and residents were left injured by a series of fires. The prime minister warned that Britain “is a tinderbox right now”, with the public set for a “difficult weekend”.
It has been a record year of wildfires in England and Wales: the number so far has passed the 1,017 recorded in 2025. Fire services declared 11 major incidents in a 24-hour period starting on Thursday.
People have been urged not to light barbecues, campfires, fireworks or anything else that could spark a blaze while the wildfire risk remains high. They have also been urged to call 999 immediately if they spot a fire.

The wildfires have also prompted calls within the Labour party to accelerate action against the climate crisis. Sadiq Khan warned Burnham not to “slow down on net zero” and said the heatwave and wildfires showed the need for action on climate change. The London mayor described the planet as being in a “deeply precarious position”.

articles.title: Hollywood actor seeks help from vicar for series
articles.raw_rss: Rev Paul Cawthorne helped Michael Sheen identify sites where toxic waste was dumped in the 1970s.
articles.raw_meta: Rev Paul Cawthorne helped Michael Sheen identify sites where toxic waste was dumped in the 1970s.
articles.jina_text:
A Shropshire vicar played a key role in a new two-part BBC documentary featuring Welsh Hollywood actor Michael Sheen's investigation into toxic waste dumps.
The Rev Paul Cawthorne, priest in charge of churches in the Hadnall area, is also a long time environmental campaigner.
He began looking into the history of the former landfill site at Stoney Hill, in Telford, where former chemical giant, Monsanto, is known to have legally dumped waste in the mid to late 1980s.
"When I found out about the Monsanto chemical dumping at Stoney Hill, I next identified Sutton Walls in Herefordshire, then Cefn Mawr in north Wales," he said.
"I then went around south Wales valleys identifying historically documented sites which needed additional testing," he added.
Cawthorne said he has been on a 20 year mission to uncover the truth.
He said that "dangerously elevated levels" of polychlorinated biphenyls - toxic man-made chemicals which don't easily break down in nature - were found in nine out of 10 sites discussed in the Buried BBC radio series.
"The results at some were literally off the scale and will have a big impact in professional circles, assuming they cannot continue to try to ignore them now," he said.
Details of Monsanto's involvement at Stoney Hill between 1985-1988, when it was managed by Shropshire County Council, was revealed in a recent Freedom of Information request.
Cawthorne has now called on the current site owners, Telford and Wrekin Council, to order a full fresh statutory investigation into the former landfill site near Coalbrookdale.
The LDRS asked Telford and Wrekin Council for a response to Cawthorne's repeated calls for an investigation.
A council spokesperson said: "Information about Stoneyhill landfill site's active management plan is available on the council's website."
The council took over the management of the former landfill site in 1998 and states on its website there is "no evidence in the records received from Shropshire County Council that toxic materials or waste were tipped in Stoneyhill landfill."
It also carries out regular testing and it states these have not identified any cause for concern.
The council's website adds that a detailed assessment and review was carried out by the Environment Agency in 2008 and "as a result the site is not considered a harm to the local environment."
For the documentary, he put his focus on the former activities of Monsanto, which produced a range of chemicals at factories in Newport, south Wales, and Ruabon, near Chirk, before the disposal legislation began to tighten in 1974.
Buried with Michael Sheen, comes to BBC Two, BBC One Wales and BBC iPlayer from Monday 17 August.
This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations.

Andy Burnham moves to cut new EV sales targets 




The UK’s biggest gigafactory has shelved plans to expand production in Sunderland because of stalled talks on a deal to supply electric car batteries to Jaguar Land Rover.
Chinese-owned AESC produces batteries for Nissan at its gigafactory next door to the Japanese carmaker’s Sunderland plant. Battery manufacturers in the UK and Europe have had a difficult few years as carmakers have retreated from previous ambitious targets to switch from internal combustion engines to electric vehicles. Several big European battery projects have gone bankrupt, while others have been forced to scale back plans in an industry dominated by Chinese players such as CATL and BYD, the world’s biggest maker of electric cars.
JLR’s sister company, Agratas, is building its own gigafactory in Somerset, England. That plant is not scheduled to start production until 2027. The Guardian in June reported that Agratas has faced construction difficulties that could delay the start of production further.

GB News hosts Dawn Neesom and Sam Francis have reacted to the "terrifying" exposure by GB News Reporter Alice Tomlinson on the takeover of London's iconic red buses by Chinese manufacturer BYD.
Detailing her report on GB News Breakfast, Alice told Dawn and Sam: "I did this investigation through an FOI request to TfL, so in 2020, there were 261 BYD buses in Londons electric vehicle bus fleet, and that has surged by 359 per cent in the last five years. 


"So now as of March 2025, that stands at almost 1,200 buses. BYD, which stands for 'Build Your Dreams' is a Chinese manufacturer. And interestingly, they have been designated by the US as a "Chinese military company". 
"BYD rejects that designation, but what it infers is that this is a company that is now essentially kind of has fingers in lots of pies in terms of London's transport system."
Reacting to the report, Dawn said: "Absolutely terrifying, it's frightening. One of the most popular e-vehicles on the road now is manufactured in China, by the Chinese, and we obviously have the mega embassy opening in London as well."
Sam then added: "It'll be interesting to find out whether it's just the capital or whether there's more widespread across the country as well, because e-vehicles are rolling out more and more and more.
"I mean, you just look around this studio, I wonder how much is probably Chinese controlled?"
Dawn concluded: "Phones, laptops, cameras, who knows?"
GB News put these exclusive findings to TfL, asking specifically whether it or its subcontracted bus operators manage these software updates and whether BYD notifies them before updates are applied.
A spokesman said: "All buses entering service in London must meet our robust technical requirements and we are committed to rigorous testing."

articles.jina_text:
Rail passengers face slower train journeys and a reduced timetable if summer heatwaves become more frequent with climate change. 
The train derailment near Lewes in East Sussex on Thursday – the hottest day of the year – has sparked fears about the potential impact of higher temperatures on the rail network. 
A second derailment happened less than 24 hours later in Essex on Friday, leading to further concern that parts of the rail infrastructure may be struggling to cope with intense weather.

 
The Labour Government may have to spend more upgrading infrastructure to help the network adapt to the changing climate, experts told The i Paper. 
The cause of Thursday’s overturned Southern Rail commuter carriages – which left 20 people injured, including two serious injuries – is not yet known. 
The cause of the partial derailment of a Greater Anglia train near Wickford in Essex is also unknown. The rear carriages were derailed in an upright position shortly after 2pm on Friday, but no injuries were initially reported. 
But heat expansion causing rail lines to buckle is one possibility that will be looked at by investigators, said industry experts.



 
Footage from Lewes revealed a section of track that the overturned train had passed over was badly warped. However, the derailing itself could have caused the movement, said experts. 
Painting rails white and ‘re-stressing’ track 
Network Rail has explained that rails are “stressed” – carefully adjusting their length to reduce tension – to help them resist the effects of high temperatures. 
“In Britain, our rails have a target stress-free temperature of 27 degrees,” Network Rail said in a post on X last month. 
Re-stressing the network for the far-higher temperatures seen this summer has not been deemed necessary because the lines also have to deal with cold temperatures in the British winter. 
However, Network Rail said it was taking steps to adjust to more severe summers: including painting rails white to reflect sunlight, fitting additional anchors to sleepers and re-stressing sections of rail lines. 

Officials investigate overturned carriages after derailment near Lewes.(Photo: James Manning/PA Wire) 
The nation’s network operator also pointed out that train speed restrictions are needed in hot weather to reduce the impact on the lines. It can mean fewer trains to avoid lines become overcrowded. 
Phil Blythe CBE, professor of intelligent transport systems at Newcastle University, said it could take “a decade or more” to adapt the UK’s rail infrastructure to extreme heat, he said.



 
Tough decisions will have to be made on priorities because “there isn’t much money around”, warned Prof Blyth – who leads the DARe hub of academics and transport industry leaders looking at climate resilience. 
Slower trains and reduced services in summer 
Passengers could face both “slower trains and reduced service” in the summers ahead “until a lot of these improvements can be made”, said Prof Blythe.

The scenes of flames completely gutting detached and semi-detached UK homes were apocalyptic, and the PM responded by temporarily banning disposable barbecues, announcing extra resources for firefighters and sending an emergency phone alert warning against “any activity that could start a fire”.

And a consultation on watering down the target for the transition to electric vehicles was announced on Friday.

‘In the heatwaves, it’s crucial’: the fight to save France’s rural swimming pools


Ageing facilities offering daily refuge face funding threat as record temperatures parch the countryside




Suzy Bernard took a breath and jumped into the deep end of her village swimming pool with a splash.
“There’s a wonderful feeling of wellbeing in the water,” said the former hospital healthcare assistant, who recently learned to swim aged 75 and was now gliding along with her daughter and grandson.



View image in fullscreen
Suzy Bernard: ‘We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives’
The municipal swimming pool, bordered by shady oak trees in the village of Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, in western France, has been the Bernard family’s daily refuge from the sweltering heatwaves this summer. Bernard is a member of the village collective, Touche Pas à Ma Piscine (Hands Off My Pool), campaigning to defend the Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe facility and calling for more government support for rural swimming pools. “We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives and stays open,” she said.


As a summer of record temperatures parched much of the French countryside, local village swimming pools, with cheap entry tickets, have often been the only shelter from the heatwaves for rural families on low incomes who cannot afford to go on holiday or who live in heat-trap homes. The pools are also crucial for teaching rural communities to swim. A total of 274 people died from drowning in France between 1 May and 15 July this year, with most deaths occurring when people jumped into rivers and waterways to cool down.





Families enjoy local swimming pools in western France


But France’s ageing rural swimming pools, many of which were built in 1970s, are in crisis as village mayors with shrinking budgets struggle to pay the high running costs and some pools are forced to close owing to lack of funds.
In Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, a village of 3,200 people in Les Hauts-d’Anjou, a farming area of the Pays de la Loire, the new mayor, Véronique Langlais, said she was determined to keep running the village pool that opened in 1973, despite an annual cost of at least €100,000 (£85,000) to the town hall’s modest budget. Three other rural pools had closed in the surrounding countryside, making this the only pool in a radius of about 20 miles.

Véronique Langlais, mayor of Hauts-d’Anjou, in the changing rooms of the Hauts-d’Anjou swimming pool

articles.jina_text:
Disposable barbecues have been temporarily banned from sale over fears they pose a "significant risk to the public" as drought and heatwave conditions continue to grip the UK.
They have been the cause of "a number of serious wildfires across the country over the summer months", the government said. 
A potential ban was first discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting in response to record temperatures earlier this week. The public have been urged not to light an open fires and to dispose of cigarettes carefully.
Meanwhile Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the country is like "a tinderbox", as 200 personnel have now been deployed to help emergency teams tackling wildfires around the country. 






Burnham says UK is like a 'tinderbox' as West Midlands crews tackle multiple fires for second day



Watch: 'Carnage' in Stourbridge as houses destroyed by fire





20 hours ago


What is causing the summer wildfires?





25 July




As part of the military deployment, Gurkha logistics teams equipped with water tankers and military engineers are now assisting fire services in South Wales. 
Andy Burnham has promised more military personnel will be deployed elsewhere if needed.
Crews in England and Wales tackled multiple blazes on Friday and an emergency alert was sent to millions of phones.
A total of 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), which matches last year's record.
As well as devastating blazes in the West Midlands which saw dozens of homes destroyed, fire crews have been in action across the two countries.
In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed.
In Hampshire, firefighters have spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, which broke out on Sunday.
Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath in the city.
On Friday evening, an emergency alert was sent to mobile phones warning of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" across England and Wales.
The message asked residents, landowners and visitors to not undertake any activity that could cause a fire "including disposable barbecues, firepits, garden incinerators of fireworks".
It was the most extensive use of the system to date, according to the government.









Disposable barbecues "cannot be considered a safe product" in the current conditions and they "must not be made available for sale either in store or online at the current time" in Great Britain, according to the advice published by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST)., external
The ban applies to England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the measures were "common-sense steps to protect lives and the environment."

PM steps up climate response with measures including better water access and support for building farm reservoirs




Farmers must not carry the risks of the climate crisis alone, Andy Burnham has said, as he announced £65m of funding to help them manage the devastating drought.
The prime minister is stepping up his response to the immediate climate crisis after facing a backlash from his own MPs and Labour’s grassroots for not addressing the climate crisis despite wildfires tearing through Britain and a drought affecting food producers. Labour MPs argued Burnham had taken too long to talk about the climate crisis and had not made it a priority.

Some farmers have had to harvest their crops early, while others are seeing low-quality produce and low yields. Most of the £65m will go to the sustainable farming incentive (SFI), which pays farmers in England to support nature. Officials have said this extra £50m will bring the total SFI budget to £290m, with extra money prioritised for areas of greatest need during the drought.
Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting on extreme heat, wildfires and drought this week. Downing Street is seeking to establish a cross-government response to the drought, bringing together action on farming, water and infrastructure, including more flexibility for food producers. Farmers who are paid to look after nature on parts of their land and are usually barred from cutting or grazing it until later in the year are now able to do so where grass is scarce, without losing payments.

articles.raw_meta: The capital sizzled with highs of 34.3 on Friday, the day after the mercury hit 38.1C in Kew Gardens
articles.jina_text:
An emergency alert from the Government was sent to millions across the UK on Friday evening, as London continued to experience baking heatwave conditions.




The alert, which began appearing on mobile devices from 7pm, warned people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks.








It comes as Friday became a record-breaking 10th day in 2026 where temperatures have exceeded 35C or more in the UK, according to the Met Office.


A screenshot of the emergency alert
PA




The capital sizzled with highs of 34.3 on Friday, the day after the hottest temperature of the year in the UK was recorded, with the mercury hitting 38.1C in Kew Gardens on Thursday.




The alert read: “There is a very high risk of wildfires nationally. Residents, landowners and visitors should not undertake any activity that could start a fire, including disposable barbecues, firepits, garden incinerators or fireworks.




“Even a small flame can rapidly develop into a major wildfire placing lives, homes, businesses and emergency responders at risk. Follow official updates and report signs of fire immediately by calling 999.”




London’s parks have been turned into “tinderbox” parched lands where fires can easily spread, including a wildfire which tore through Hornchurch Country Park on Friday evening.


An aerial view of a parched golf course in in Mitcham, London
Getty




The London Fire Brigade (LFB) confirmed that 14 fire engines and around 90 firefighters responded to the blaze, which produced a significant amount of smoke.












Sir Sadiq Khan has urged Londoners to create fire breaks in their gardens to protect their homes, while the London Fire Brigade (LFB) has also warned of the dangers that major blazes could start in people’s gardens.




More than 1,000 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), the same as last year’s record-breaking total. 








Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, said that the alert was “the most extensive use of the UK’s emergency alert system in response to an active incident”.









The alert played havoc with TV and radio broadcasts, with the One Show’s 20th anniversary special episode disrupted just minutes after starting.

Burnham criticised for EV and North Sea approach amid climate crisis


Cut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO2 to emissions in UK, say green campaigners




Andy Burnham has been criticised for moving to cut electric vehicle (EV) sales targets and accept North Sea drilling at a time of devastating wildfires caused by the climate emergency.
The prime minister for the first time acknowledged on Friday that the climate crisis was behind hundreds of wildfires that have ripped across the parts of the UK.

The scale of the disaster has prompted the government to bring in the military, ban the sale of disposable barbecues and activate the national alert system to issue safety advice to people across England and Wales in areas at risk on Friday night.
However, Burnham was also accused of failing to take the push for net zero seriously enough, as the government took steps towards watering down EV targets on the same day.


View image in fullscreen
Several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands were destroyed as a result of wildfires this week. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images
The government on Friday launched a consultation on cutting the target for new EVs to as little as 50% of all new cars in 2030, down from 80% under existing rules, in proposals that could add millions of tonnes a year to the UK’s carbon dioxide emissions.


The consultation will include several options, including leaving the headline target unchanged, or cutting it to 70%, 60% or 50%.
In a video from the West Midlands, where homes have been destroyed and dozens of people injured, Burnham appeared to acknowledge the seriousness of the climate crisis. “We cannot accept this as the new normal,” he said. “This isn’t happening in isolation.
“Much of England and Wales is in drought and we are in another period of extreme heat. Farmers are watching crops fail and firefighters have faced hundreds of wildfires in a matter of weeks. This is what climate change looks like, here and now.”


View image in fullscreen
Andy Burnham and the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, right, with the West Midlands chief fire officer, Simon Tuhill, during a visit to Stourbridge on Friday. Photograph: Peter Byrne/Reuters


But in a broadcast interview, he also defended his “pragmatic” approach on extracting oil and gas from the North Sea. His government will shortly have to decide whether to allow new drilling at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields, with a consultation on the former closing on Monday.

‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfires


Thursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’




People in Stourbridge have described the fires that devastated more than a dozen homes as “horrendous” and “distressing”, with one describing blazes that surpassed the height of residential houses.
Multiple fires spread across the West Midlands on Thursday as temperatures reached record highs of 38.1C in the UK, during the country’s fifth consecutive heatwave.

Fifty-four people, including 19 who were taken to hospital, were treated at eight different fires on Thursday, West Midlands ambulance service said, with the fire service confirming 19 homes in Stourbridge, a market town in Dudley, had been fully destroyed and an additional 18 damaged.
During a visit to Stourbridge on Friday, Andy Burnham said the UK was like a “tinderbox” and announced the commission of firefighting planes to tackle future wildfires. “I’ve never seen scenes like this anywhere in Britain,” he told the BBC.
The Guardian spoke to people who were forced to hurriedly evacuate from their homes in Stourbridge on Thursday, as a wildfire spread near the town’s golf course.


View image in fullscreen
From left: Andy Hobbs, Gemma Hobbs and neighbour John Bairner, were evacuated from their homes on Osmaston Road. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian
They repeatedly praised the support and efforts of local authorities and neighbours, but are yet to return home, with some staying at a nearby hotel or a makeshift evacuation centre that had been set up at a local boarding school.


Gemma Hobbs, 46, and her partner, Andy, 61, were evacuated from their home on Osmaston Road on Thursday, as the wildfires raged over a mile away. Andy described seeing a house in flames.
Gemma said: “I looked out the windows and all I could see was thick black smoke. My husband came home in a bit of a flap and said: ‘We’ve got to get out. We’ve got to get out immediately.’”
Andy added: “It’s just the fact you don’t expect something to be as exponential as this so quickly. From the span of the area, it’s over 40 acres, that’s what we’ve been told.”

articles.title: Electric vehicle sales targets could be cut after pressure from car makers
articles.raw_rss: The government says it is considering cutting the new electric car sales target from 80% to 50% by 2030.
articles.raw_meta: The government says it is considering cutting the new electric car sales target from 80% to 50% by 2030.
articles.jina_text:
The UK's electric vehicle (EV) sales target could be cut after the government launched a review following pressure from car makers.
Currently, manufacturers must ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.
The government has now said it is considering cutting that figure to as far as 50% of all sales by the end of the decade, which it will consult on until late October.
Environmental groups have argued that watering down the target undermines the UK's long-term climate goals.
Under the current policy, known as the ZEV mandate, the percentage of new car sales that need to be EVs increases each year, from 33% for 2026 until it reaches 80% by 2030. It started at 22% in 2024.
An outright ban on selling purely petrol or diesel cars past 2030 will stay in place, something that Labour promised in its election manifesto.
However the changes now being consulted on could allow car makers to sell more hybrid vehicles as a proportion of the UK's overall sales.
That means if the government drops pure electric sales targets to 50%, the other 50% would need to be hybrid.
Another option would be keeping the target at 80% but with flexibility for car makers extending as far as 2034.
A longer term deadline for phasing out new hybrid sales would also remain in place for 2035.
The policy on EV sales has already changed a lot over the years.
A ban on selling new petrol and diesel vehicles by 2030 was first announced by Boris Johnson when he was prime minister, then pushed back to 2035 by his successor Rishi Sunak.
Sunak also introduced more gradual targets for EV sales under the ZEV mandate.
Labour has previously accused previous Conservative governments of "moving goalposts on phase out dates".
It comes after motor industry figures urged ministers to ease the targets, arguing that demand for electric vehicles isn't yet high enough, and meeting them is costing manufacturers too much money.
That is despite electric cars making up a quarter of total sales in the UK over the first seven months of the year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).
The Climate Change Committee, which advises the government, has said switching from diesel and petrol engines to EVs will be the most effective way of cutting carbon emissions over the next decade.
Transport Secretary, Heidi Alexander said on Friday: "It's right we keep targets under review to ensure they're practical and back British industry. 
"The end goal hasn't changed – but we need to take business with us on the journey, and that's exactly what we're doing today, by making sure industry has the chance to shape how we get there."
Lisa Brankin, managing director of Ford of Britain, welcomed the government's "willingness to listen" to car makers, adding: "It is vital to give the industry and customers the certainty that we need."

‘High coral cover is evidence of recovery and resilience, not evidence that the disturbances causing mortality didn’t happen,’ scientist says 
 
 





The Australian newspaper appeared to think it had a slam-dunk this week with a front page story pointing to official government data which showed “the Great Barrier Reef is refusing to die” despite decades of warnings that global heating would cause its demise.
In an editorial to back its reporting, the newspaper claimed the “continued good health” of the reef was a “welcome reminder that physics rather than the pseudo-religion of climate change doom still holds sway over the natural order.”

Scientific-based assessments of risks facing the reef from global heating were wrong, it seemed, and the data and the physics showed it.
But the Australian Institute of Marine Science – the agency upon which the outlet pinned its claims – has told this column the newspaper was guilty of “oversimplified framing” and that its recent surveys did not contradict warnings about the risks to the reef from the climate crisis.


“The scientific concern is not that the GBR should already have disappeared, it’s whether reefs will have sufficiently long periods between disturbances for full ecosystem recovery,” the institute said.
The Guardian sent questions to The Australian but received no response.
‘Volatility is evidence of ecosystem instability’
The Australian’s report leaned heavily on the latest annual results of the institute’s long-term monitoring program – a 40-year effort which, between August 2025 and June 2026, took detailed records from surveys of 121 reefs.
The program reports annually on levels of coral cover – that is, how much live hard coral is growing on reef areas – which was at “near record levels” across the reef, The Australian reported.

The Prime Minister was speaking as he visited the scene of a fire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands, where residents were forced to evacuate.

        







The Prime Minister said the drought could be followed by flooding as heavy rain falls of dry ground (Jacob King/PA)




David Lynch
2 minutes ago







Flooding could follow the wildfires sweeping the country, Andy Burnham has said.




The Prime Minister made the warning as he visited the scene of a fire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands, where residents were forced to evacuate.




A total of 54 people have been treated by paramedics, including 19 who were admitted to hospital, after wildfires broke out across the region.








Speaking to broadcasters on Friday afternoon, the Prime Minister paid tribute to the work of firefighters, and added: “We might be in for a wet autumn and winter straight after this, because of El Nino and some of the issues there, which was reported to Cobra. So, after fire could come floods.




“We have to face up to the changing climate. I think we need a different debate about that. There’s no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy. We need to see that transition accelerate. Those are all of the issues that, you know, are right now in discussion.




“But the Cobra meeting earlier this week, I think has enabled us to mobilise resource today to individuals, to communities, and to our fire and rescue services, and we’re very, very grateful to them.”




Mr Burnham later told the BBC that the Met Office believes the dry spell will last until the end of September, when some rain is expected.




He also told the broadcaster: “Maybe some rainfall, but not as much as we need, and then we are heading straight into a very, very wet latter part of the year, where the risk of flooding will be maybe greater because of the dry ground conditions.


Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited the scene of a fire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands on Friday (Peter Byrne/PA)
PA Wire




“At the moment, fire and rescue services are not set up for flooding properly, and again, these are questions that I have to take away, and you know I won’t shy away from them.”













Met Office climate spokesman Grahame Madge said it was a “tremendously tricky job” to work out which climate drivers will be the most dominant ahead of autumn and winter.




Mr Madge told the Press Association: “But the Prime Minister is perfectly right in what he said, in terms of there is a known association between strong El Nino events and a wet autumn.









“It’s important to highlight that El Nino is a pattern of natural climate variability – it’s not linked to climate change per se.




“It can accentuate other climate signals, such as a warmer atmosphere, it can hold more moisture, all of that, but it’s not an artefact of climate change itself.”

articles.jina_text:
Five key reservoirs across England and Wales are “exceptionally low” as drought and extreme heat piles pressure on public water supply that is likely to continue into the autumn.
Most of Europe has endured back-to-back climate crisis-driven heatwaves this summer. The extreme heat, coupled with strikingly little rainfall, means almost three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales is now in drought.

Environment Agency data from 11 August shows five key reservoirs are now “exceptionally low”.
Wimbleball reservoir, operated by South West Water, is less than half full, at 46%. The other four that are “exceptionally low” are Clatworthy in Somerset (48%), Hanningfield in Essex (56%), Clywedog in Powys (56%), and the Dove group in Derbyshire (69%).

Across England, total reservoir levels have fallen to 66%, down from 69% last week and nearly 14 percentage points lower than expected for this time of year. Of the 32 reservoirs the Environment Agency classifies as strategically important or geographically representative, just four are classed as at normal levels.


These are Draycote Water in Warwickshire, Bewl in Kent, Roadford in Devon and Vyrnwy in Powys.
Reservoirs are essential for the security of water supply, providing drinking water to millions of people.
In its latest summary published on Thursday, the National Hydrological Monitoring Programme said aridity in July had been “unprecedented” and that “widespread below-normal to exceptionally low” water flows were likely to persist well into the autumn, with “further deterioration” likely.


View image in fullscreen
Woodhead reservoir near Manchester. Photograph: Jon Super/AP


Alastair Chisholm, the lead for water policy, regulation and governance at the consultancy firm Arup, said with three droughts recorded in the past five years, the country was in “new territory”.
During last year’s drought, reservoir levels also fell to extremely low levels. By this time last year, the Pennines group and Yorkshire group reservoirs were less than 39% full, and experts say this cumulative impact is of particular concern.
England and Wales rely on on reservoirs filling up over the winter – and this year’s particularly wet winter has meant the situation this summer is not as bad as it could have been. “If we do get a dry winter this time round, then that will be very concerning for the government,” Chisholm said.

Prof Liz Bentley, the chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said the key concern now was how long the dry weather would continue.
“There is very little rain forecast over the next couple of weeks and that is more the concern. If we go through autumn and winter and have low rainfall, we could have real trouble,” she said.
Mark Smith, the chair of the Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management’s water resources specialist panel, said that while winter rain helped, “ultimately you can only store so much”.

articles.title: France and England battle multiple wildfires as record heat grips Europe
articles.raw_rss: Firefighters across France and central England are battling multiple fires as a new wave of record-breaking heat hits Europe
articles.raw_meta: Firefighters across France and central England are battling multiple fires as a new wave of record-breaking heat hits Europe
articles.jina_text:
Firefighters across France and in central England struggled against multiple fires Friday as a new wave of record-breaking heat baked a swath of Europe, their task further complicated by exceptionally parched landscapes.
With France experiencing its driest year ever, a new fire raced through woodlands overnight in the Landes region on the southwest coast. The blaze forced more than 500 people to evacuate their homes in the town of Luglon as hundreds of firefighters deployed to the area, the regional administration said Friday.
It’s one of several fires scorching forests around France this week, including in normally cooler and wetter regions in the north and Brittany. A historic fire devoured forests near Bordeaux last month and pushed a quarter of a million people from their homes.





After the U.K. recorded its hottest day of the year, wildfires raced across the West Midlands and saw several houses burned to the ground. They have been “one of the most significant” incidents the region’s fire service has ever dealt with, chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said. 
Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data from the National Fire Chiefs Council.

The fires came on the hottest day of the year, when temperatures reached 38.1 degrees Celsius (100.6 degrees Fahrenheit) in west London.


In France, temperatures Thursday approached 41 C (106 F) in several areas, from Aquitaine in the southwest to the Rhone River valley in the east, according to the national weather service. They were forecast to reach similar levels Friday before dropping over the weekend. 
The historic temperatures are linked to human-caused climate change, and are hitting countries more designed for long cold seasons and ill-equipped for this sort of heat, with limited air conditioning.



In northern Greece, more than 300 vacationers and residents were evacuated by sea Thursday after a wildfire swept through a pine forest and threatened seaside homes, authorities said.

Farmers in South Korea, meanwhile, are reporting that potatoes are “boiling” in the hard, parched, heated ground before they could be harvested. “It’s not just one or two fields like this,” a farmer told the Japanese news agency SBS. “How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting.” 
So, your shopping basket will get more expensive. But how much more expensive? Most of the burden will fall on retailers. The price rises we will see in the shops in the coming weeks and months as these poor harvests feed through to the shelves will not be anything like as big as the increase in the wholesale price. This is the price at which retailers buy produce from farmers, and it includes significant costs for packaging, transport, storage and labour. But price rises at the shops will still be significant.



 
A study by the University of East Anglia indicates that a 10 per cent rise in wholesale fruit and vegetable prices could translate into an increase of around 1 to 2 per cent at the checkout, depending on the crop and the time period. This implies that somewhere in the region of 10 to 20 per cent of the rise in the wholesale price is typically passed on to the consumer. 
Data on wholesale prices is patchy with government figures only covering a fairly small selection of “barometer” foods. But these do give a good early indication of how things will change as summers get hotter and hotter.

articles.jina_text:

View image in fullscreen
People in Jorhat, Assam, wade through floodwaters with animals and belongings salvaged after flooding in late July.  Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images


‘We feared we’d all be drowned’: the Indian floods that killed more than 100 and left thousands homeless


More than 2,600 villages have been flooded in Assam this year, in a climate disaster made worse by uncontrolled deforestation and mining in the region




It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.

“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.


View image in fullscreen
Gitali Phukon in flood water outside her house on 28 July, a week after the village was flooded.  Photograph: Gitali Phukon/The Migration Story
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.

articles.title: My one-year postgrad degree will cost me £30,000 and leave me struggling to buy a home
articles.raw_rss: James Fenneberg, 45, says the money he is putting into his education could otherwise have gone towards building greater financial security
articles.raw_content:
At 45, James Fenneberg is going back to university for a postgraduate degree, and anticipates it will cost him around £30,000 in fees, renting, travel and materials costs.



James is studying a postgraduate degree in environmental architecture at the Royal College of Art (RCA) in London, starting in September, but worries the cost of the degree will lead to him struggling to buy a property in the south of England, where he wants to live.



Though he will get a student loan, it will only cover around £13,000 of his fees – and he’ll be left repaying the cost for up to 30 years, at a rate of 6 per cent on all his earnings over £21,000.





It also won’t cover his living costs and so bar a £5,000 bursary, he will be left dipping into inheritance he received from a family member – which he’d previously earmarked for a house purchase of his own.



He plans to work during his degree if he can, and hopes the qualification will allow him to find employment as a designer focused on climate change. He says the course is “unique”, which is why he is not considering studying in a cheaper city.



But he is still concerned about how the burden of the debt and upfront costs will affect him in the future, highlighting the dilemmas many who take on higher education debt face.



James currently lives in Thurrock, Kent, but will have to move to London for his qualification, which will cost him around £1,000 a month in rent and bills.

articles.jina_text:
Orangutans rescued from wildlife traffickers face a new threat from the record number of fires that have broken out in Indonesia in recent weeks.
Flames have come within metres of an animal rehabilitation centre in West Kalimantan as hot, dry and windy conditions have been amplified by a powerful El Niño and the human-driven climate crisis.

In the first 13 days of August, Indonesia registered more than three times more forest fire hotspots than in the whole of the same month last year. This followed a record number of blazes between January and July.
West Kalimantan has been at the epicentre. After 40 days without rain, there have been dozens of severe outbreaks of fire in the region.


View image in fullscreen
Orangutans at the Yiari rehabilitation centre. Photograph: Yiari
Flames threatened the Yiari orangutan rehabilitation centre this week. The fire moved rapidly from 1km away to within 100 metres of the perimeter within days, prompting staff to relocate the 60 resident orangutans to enclosures in the middle of the centre.







‘Should we leave them to die?’ The battle over how to save orangutans from the curse of palm oil

Read more
Indonesia authorities have water-bombed the forest to try to control the blaze, and teams from the centre joined the firefighting efforts as the air quality worsened, posing a threat to animals and the wider ecosystem.


The centre’s director, Dr Karmele Llano Sánchez, said in her latest update that battling the fire had been relentless. “We were fighting it until 3am, but this morning it has reignited. The teams are working round the clock but they are exhausted.”
The situation had reportedly stabilised as of Thursday evening, with all the animals safe, but the meteorological agency has said the hot, dry conditions are likely to continue and could lead to more outbreaks.
Indonesian authorities have urged people to avoid setting fires and to remain vigilant because the peak of the fire season is usually in September and October.
Yiari is seeking funds for more firefighting equipment. It warned of the growing threat earlier this year after a fire started for land clearing spread into one of its ecosystem restoration sites.

Romania shuts its last nuclear reactor as drought-hit Danube river drops to record low


Cernavoda shutdown poses immediate problems for Moldova, which relies on Romanian power ​to cover its own electricity shortages




Romania has been forced to shut down the last working ⁠reactor at its only nuclear plant after drought caused the Danube river to fall to record lows – a rare move that will immediately affect power supplies in neighbouring Moldova.
Drought and record-low water levels have deepened fears of an energy crisis across Europe, which is facing a new summer heatwave.

The drought-hit Danube, whose waters cool the Romanian plant in Cernavoda, already forced Nucelarelectrica to shut down ⁠one reactor ​in late July.






Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous
Yiannis Baboulias


Read more
On Thursday the company said it needed to shut the second reactor “due to the significant and ongoing drop” in the river’s water level, and it did not foresee a restart in within the next 10 days. Nuclearelectrica’s two 706-megawatt reactors account for 20% of the country’s power ⁠output.
Romania has declared a state of energy emergency throughout August and asked companies and households to reduce consumption during peak hours.
Shutting down the reactor posed immediate problems for Moldova, Romania’s eastern neighbour, ⁠which has also endured low river levels and relies on Romanian power ​to cover up to 60% ​of its own electricity shortages.
With Romanian ​imports now unavailable, Moldova faces the prospect of increased purchases from Ukraine, ​if Kyiv can supply the ‌power, buying more ​expensive power from ​western countries or imposing rolling power cuts.


“I think we should be ready for a worsening situation, including power outages, although it’s hard to say for sure right now,” Moldovan energy expert Sergiu Tofilat told Radio Chisinau.
Romania’s energy ministry said it had ⁠turned on a 330-megawatt lignite-fired power plant, adding it was also relying on increased ​wind generation and hydro power – based ‌on available water in reservoirs – to ‌make up for shortages.
It has warned that as a last resort, large industrial users would have to face restrictions in the evening hours to save electricity. In early August, the government said carmakers Dacia and Ford would pause production in the country until 19 August to help with the power deficit.

articles.jina_text:
The floods that have killed 103 people in the north-eastern Indian state of Assam this summer were not made worse by the climate crisis, but rather more immediate human errors such as unchecked deforestation and poor flood defences, a new analysis has found. 
The death toll continued to rise in Assam in Thursday’s update on the flooding, which began in late June across the northern part of the state, with multiple rivers remaining above danger levels. The floods have displaced more than 700,000 people and submerged vast stretches of farmland. Although many residents have begun returning to their homes as floodwaters recede, at least 49,000 remain housed in 125 relief camps and distribution centres, officials said earlier this week.
The loss of animal life has also been stark, with tens of thousands of farm animals and pets washed away, according to the Assam State Disaster Management Authority. With cattle sheds and grazing land badly inundated, the floods will have a long-lasting impact on livelihoods in a region heavily dependent on livestock for incomes, said Sneha Ganguly of the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, a co-author of the new study.





The floods also exposed weaknesses in Assam’s healthcare system, cutting off primary care clinics behind submerged roads, interrupting medicine supplies to people with long-term conditions and raising the risk of disease outbreaks in crowded relief camps.
The rainfall that set off the flooding was ordinary by the standards of the region, according to World Weather Attribution, an international team that assesses the role of global warming in extreme weather. 

Downpours of that size are expected roughly every one to two years, they found. However, what turned routine monsoon rain into a disaster that displaced hundreds of thousands and submerged 45,000 hectares of cropland was the state of the land it fell on. 


"Unplanned urbanisation, deforestation, poor drainage, inadequate structural flood management measures, and other anthropogenic changes now outweigh natural rainfall variability in explaining flood frequency," said Ms Ganguly.
"While climate change is making life harder for most Indians, not every disaster is a climate change disaster," said Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London and another co-author. 



"The devastating flooding in Assam was instead driven by extreme human exposure, environmental degradation, and infrastructure limitations."
Assam lies in the floodplain of the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia, which rises on the Tibetan plateau and descends through the eastern Himalayas carrying enormous quantities of sediment.

articles.jina_text:
Adding huge quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere is set to cause the Earth’s forests to wither and die rather than flourish, according to a new study that counters erroneous claims that fossil fuel pollution will green the planet.
An analysis of fossilized leaf cells from a period known as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (or PETM), which occurred about 56m years ago, has helped reconstruct how the world’s forests responded when planet-heating gases were previously being released at a rapid rate.

The current galloping pace of carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels is unmatched in historic and prehistoric records but the PETM, when huge amounts of carbon were released over a 130,000-year period and the world heated up by as much as 8C (14F), is the closest comparison.
The authors of the new paper found this prehistoric change caused a retreat in the forests that blanketed the Paleocene-Eocene world, causing them to die off as the Earth browned rather than greened, a finding they state has “chilling implications” for today’s world.


View image in fullscreen
Fragments of fossilized leaves like these helped the authors re-create the forest canopies of 56m years ago. Photograph: Dr Regan Dunn
“What we see is that as the carbon dioxide ramped up, the forests became very dense but then subsequently collapsed, opening up dramatically,” said Regan Dunn, a researcher at La Brea Tar Pits and the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, who led the study.


“Around 60% of the biomass of the standing vegetation was gone; it was a huge loss. This should be a concern because the rate of carbon release has never been higher than now.”
Dun added: “Forests are some of our best friends and allies but we are already seeing them die back, be cut down and consumed by wildfires. It’s happening quickly; every summer the change seems faster and faster.”







Trees may store less planet-heating carbon than hoped, study suggests

Read more
Plants like trees require carbon to build their structures and, along with water and sunlight, provide food. Once the world started to burn coal, oil and gas in huge volumes from the industrial revolution onwards, the amount of emitted carbon dioxide surged at an unprecedented rate, with atmospheric concentrations of CO2 rising by more than 50% in little over a century.
This increase in carbon did initially help boost some plant life, a change that has been seized upon by those who question the facts of climate science. Prominent figures in Donald Trump’s administration have argued that burning fossil fuels is good for the environment.
“CO2 was never a pollutant,” Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, told Fox Business earlier this year as the federal government moved to erase its own power to address the climate crisis. “When we breathe, we emit CO2. Plants need CO2 to survive and grow. They thrive with more CO2.”
